utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, I'll return to your views on Seselj later. We'd reached the beginning of 1990. I'm not going to trouble the Chamber to remind themselves with the view of the Slovenian and Croatian walkout of the 14th Congress. But can you just help me with this on the rejection of Slovenia's amendments. What was the amendment, if you can remember, that was the last proposed amendment before the Slovenians walked out?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it something that had to do with doing away with torture in Yugoslavia, and that was the amendment that was proposed and that was rejected? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was about any kind of torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Am I the only one whose LiveNote isn't working at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've seen approach of Raskovic at tab 2 already -- not tab 2 but at a document we looked at yesterday. But let's move on in 1990. On the 27th of June, amongst the municipalities that declared themselves for independence was Benkovac; correct? We can look at the document, if necessary, but you should be able to remember this.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that because I was not a member of the Municipal Assembly of Benkovac. However, I think it was not about independence. It may have been about association at the level of an association of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we've got the document. It's 351, tab 8. But I want to know this, please: By this time, which is June of 1990 - that's why we're looking at things chronologically - there had been no violence, had there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. There had been violence. In my previous responses, I have already said that throughout Croatia, monuments sacred to the Serbs had been attacked. I mentioned Split and other places, and this was all before June. Even in 1989, a Politika kiosk in Osijek was blown up. International newspapers reported this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see -- pause -- pause --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had started earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've seen, of course, already the development of hate talk on both sides. You've told us about what the Croats said, and I don't deny that they said terrible things, and we've started to see what was being said on your side. What I want to know is had killings or anything of that sort started or are we dealing at this stage with a different level of civil disturbance?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, as regards murders, there had been pressure, and in early 1991 there was a murder. In 1990, however --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were attacks but not murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... responsive to the question. We're dealing with events by June 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have time to look at it. It's 351, tab 8 is the document which is the Association of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, what I'm going to suggest to you is that there was a determination, led by whoever we'll discover, but there was a determination to have ethnic separation well before significant violence happened. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't accept it because there had been violence. You haven't allowed me to finish my response. On the 18th of May, 1990, in Benkovac, there was an attempted murder of Miroslav Mlinar. He had been stabbed with a knife. And you're saying there hadn't been any attacks. Well, this is an evident example. As far as I know, the Serbian Democratic Party suspended its relations with the Croatian parliament and did not attend the parliamentary sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what we heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I find that question ambiguous. When you talk about a determination to have ethnic separation well before significant violence, do you mean on the part of the Croats or on the part of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the part of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the way the witness understood it, however I must say I didn't immediately understand it in view of the evidence we've been listening to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let's move on, if we may. But Babic has given evidence in this court. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about that, yes, from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he explained to us that he sought and got support both from Jovic and from this accused. Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I think that is an untruth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babic is not a reliable man. He's a man who would say anything if it was in his interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So you make that point. What do you say is in Jovic's interest to have explained that he was given support -- in Babic's interest to say he was given support by Jovic and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- I don't know him well, but as far as I know, he never said that before, and I don't know what kind of help he would have got in 1990. He was in power in Knin. He had been elected as a member of the SDS, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is, again, chronologically interesting or significant and I want your help with it. He has told us that it was on the 13th of August that he went, Babic went, to the accused and got his support. It's a matter of considerable detail what he's told us about it, but he told -- he told us he would have the support of the accused, and that's what he was told by the accused. Now, you tell us something about the so-called log revolution. Whose idea was that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk about the log revolution. Let me tell you about the 13th of August. You put your question and then you move on to something else. Mr. Babic said that he had been to see the accused. I don't see any reason for that. The SDS had its deputies in the parliament. I don't know what sort of help he would have wanted. As for the so-called log revolution, it was not a log revolution. As I said yesterday, after the 17th of August, that is after the arrival of the Croatian paramilitary formations and the first attack from Korenica in the direction of Benkovac, the people of Lika put logs across the roads, and that's all. The people were attempting to defend their homes from the illegal paramilitary formations. They were trying to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause for a minute --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were armed. They had personnel carriers and, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Babic has told us that at that meeting on the 13th, he was told by the accused that he'd have the support of the army and that he was advised by the federal minister of the interior to erect barricades, so the business of erecting barricades, logs, came from Belgrade. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Babic had never said anything like that before or thought anything like that. Why he's saying that now, well, that's up to him, but the log revolution started or, rather, barricades were put up because the Croatian paramilitary formations had attacked the Serbian people. And you have an example of this in Benkovac. I don't believe anyone from Belgrade, especially the army, told him to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do you accept at all -- no, let's go back. You've said that Babic is unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nice, that the truth has to be established here. It's not time that's at stake but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, you choose to say that Babic is unreliable. Let me just tell you a couple of things. He's pleaded guilty on the basis of facts set out by the Prosecution at a public hearing. Included in the facts set out and on the basis of which he pleaded guilty are indeed that he went and saw this accused on the 13th of August, got the offers of support that he was -- he told us about in evidence, and he explains how there was then a parallel structure comprising members of the Ministry of the Interior and the state security supporting events in the Krajina. He's gone on to explain about the different position of him and Martic - you may have heard of this in the press, I don't know - and he's explained how there was an objective called a joint criminal enterprise -- or he pleaded guilty on this basis, the purpose of which was the forcible removal of the majority of Croats from non-Serb population. So he's given evidence, he's pleaded guilty on that basis, and he's been sentenced to a long period of imprisonment. Now, what is it that you can point to before we look at the next piece of evidence that says that Mr. Babic is incorrect when he says that Gracanin advised him to set up barricades?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's my opinion that his whole testimony is incorrect. Why? In 1990, Mr. Nice, there were no parallel organs of authority. Mr. Babic was in power. He had been legally elected in the Municipal Assembly. Nobody was setting up a new parallel government. Mr. Zecevic was in Benkovac as a member of the SDS. He had been elected quite lawfully. So what kind of parallel authorities would there be? The MUP was operating quite normally. The only problem was that the Croatian paramilitary formations, the so-called Zengas, tried to attack Serb villages and disarm police stations where the Serbs were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it fair to cut him short when your question is twice as long as the answer so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness seems to me to be giving relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Atlagic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The inquiry is why Babic should not be believed, why he's unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, as far as I know, and to the extent of my previous contacts with him, which were not extensive, he's a person who would do anything if he even had a small interest in doing it. He is a person whom you cannot trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I think Babic is saying this either because someone told him to say it or because he's been blackmailed, because none of it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. I want you now, please -- we'll distribute them, a short passage from the film called "The Death of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've had problems with, as we know, the transcripts provided and the text put on the screen, so if the interpreters are able to assist us with an interpretation of the language as they hear it, I'd be very grateful. Now, we've all got the transcript. It's a Sanction, if the booth would deal with it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the man Gracanin, described as a federal police minister in the text that we have, and I'd like you to listen to what he said about this part of the history. Play it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] To put up barricades. I taught them to do that, and to keep guard at night with any weapons they had. They had hunting weapons at least. They had to keep guard. The villagers had to be constantly vigilant in order to prevent an incursion by the Ustasha. "The promises given by Mr. Jovic I felt would be helpful in some way. I thought they could help us somehow. "Armed with more than advice, the Serbs from Knin organised roadblocks. Belgrade Television was quick to play on the fears of their Serb brothers in Croatia. "3.30. We are at a position where guard is being kept. The people are scared."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will be enough, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points, please: Starting with the last part of that clip, did you see television broadcasts showing people being stopped at roadblocks, expressing their fears?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me say that what I saw on the footage, I don't know what time it was filmed, I mean the part with Mr. Gracanin, but if it was after the 17th of August, 1990, then it was quite logical for barricades to be put up, because the policemen had already attacked by then, especially in September when more than one municipality had been attacked by illegal formations who are attacking the Serbian people. So people even took hunting weapons to defend their homes and their hearths. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the last part. We'll come back to the first part. Were broadcasts of people expressing fear at road -- at checkpoints put out by the media? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, try again, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were broadcasts of people expressing fear at checkpoints put out by the media?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw on television, of course there was fear when there were roadblocks. Both Serbs and Croats were afraid, but they were afraid of the policemen. The barricades were close to Serbian villages in order to provide protection from the paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming back to the first part of that clip, do you have any reason to doubt now what Babic has said about being advised by Gracanin and taught, indeed, as Gracanin puts it, to use roadblocks in the log revolution so-called?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that Gracanin told him that at the time. Logs were put up later, after the attack of the Croatian policemen on the rally in Benkovac. That very night the Serbs from Lika put up barricades to prevent armed special units with three vehicles coming into Benkovac against those people. I don't believe Gracanin said that. I can't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I be clear about what Mr. Babic has allegedly promised to -- I'm sorry, Mr. Jovic is allegedly to have promised to Mr. Babic? In the transcript we received in written form, it says -- it's about Mr. Babic's order: "We did not get a specific promise, but I was left in no doubt that Belgrade would help us."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But our transcript says otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, we know from these -- these experiences with this film that what appears on the screen should be disregarded and we should rely on what is said by the interpreters. And what they provided us with, "The promises given by Mr. Jovic I felt would be helpful in some way, I thought they could help us some way, armed with more than advice --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's narrative, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's substantially different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But it's the first part that's the most important part for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You still believe it's a film you ought to be relying on, do you, in view of the tendentious nature of much of the commentary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where there is -- I certainly do. Where somebody is speaking directly to the camera and giving his account, like Gracanin does on this occasion, it's extremely valuable, because there is no reason to doubt that he said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's edited, Mr. Nice. You have to wonder about how it's been put together and what's been selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We still rely on it and seek to do so. And on this occasion, of course, it fits with the evidence that has been given by the witness Mr. Babic. Can we move into private session to deal with a protected document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Isn't the truth that the log -- by the time of the log revolution on the 17th of August, 1990, again there had been no substantial violence committed in terms of deaths and killings on either side and that this was the first act of force used in the dispute between Croatia and the Serbs living in Croatia? This is the first act of force, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the first act of violence, although there had been attempts at violence before. It's like you were not listening to me or you don't want to hear it. On the 18th of May, 1990, in Benkovac, Miroslav Mlinar, who was a member of the SDS, was stabbed, and the president of the SDS froze their party relations with the Croatian Assembly, after which they did not appear in the Croatian Assembly for another month. They started participating again only a month later. So there have been assaults even before that. I've spoken about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... adequately this witness. I'll change my system. Hearing this witness adequately. I'm going to suggest to you -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat if Mr. Nice hasn't heard me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no need to repeat it. Mr. Nice has it on the screen and he has read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another piece of information that is relevant to 1990. That is in November policemen Goran Galavanja [phoen] was killed in place called Karince [phoen], so that was another assault. He was killed in that village, and I think there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is after August 1990. But before August, in my area, there was only the case of Miroslav Mlinar who was stabbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have that point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, I'm going to suggest -- I'm going to suggest to you one way and another that the Serbs in Croatia, in seeking ethnic separation, were in part or whole responding to the agendas of others even if you didn't know it at the time, and discovering yourselves erecting barricades on the advice from Belgrade may be one example of it. Do you accept that you may have been responding to agendas coming from Belgrade unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't accept that. I can't accept what you're trying to insinuate. As for ethnic association among Serbs, it was the Croats who sought ethnic separation before. And I told you about the documents of the Croatian Democratic Union and their political platform and their election campaign even before the election. The Croats separated from Yugoslavia and from Serbia even before they were elected. And my colleagues of Croat ethnicity told me this after the victory of the HDZ, "We are no longer brothers or friends." And when the amendments were passed, they told me we haven't been friends ever since the amendments. It was a process, the separation of Croatia from Yugoslavia, and in parallel the Serbs were also trying to exercise their right to separate from Croatia because they were not managing even to gain cultural autonomy that they sought through the parliament, for instance. You can look at my contributions in the work of the parliament. I was saying that Serbs were seeking autonomy, and as --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the developments continued, the ambitions of the Serbian Democratic Party also developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know that there are audibility problems in the newly designed courtroom. I'm doing my best to accommodate the interpreters today by change of the way we're working. I'm going to try it with both microphones and ask them if that helps. Apparently it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on to 1991. The declaration of the RSK occurred in steps starting in December -- being completed in 1991, but let's just look at you, Mr. Atlagic. In 1991, groups developed of Serbs who were absolutely opposed to violence and to the war option. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Serbs, they were in general opposed to the war option. They resisted it. They were not trying to cause war. It was the Croat paramilitary formations who caused war, and of course peace was more in their interest, not war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the specific groups, one was the Serb Democratic Forum, and in 1991, it's right, isn't it, that you initially attended some of their meetings? You never joined up, but you attended some of their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out the possibility that I attended, just like I attended meetings of the HDZ in Benkovac when Mr. Tudjman spoke to them, et cetera. However, I'm not really familiar with the activities of the Serb Democratic Forum in 1991. I don't remember that, and I don't know who led the forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Pupovac, a much respected and continuing elected politician in Croatia would have been there, for one, and he and his colleagues maintained throughout the position -- sorry? Go on.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- in fact, I'm 100 per cent sure that I didn't see Mr. Pupovac in 1991 at any meeting in the area of Serb Krajina. As far as I know, he never came there. Dr. Zarko Puhovski was the only one who came and who organised these meetings and spoke against the war, and that is where I had been. As for Mr. Pupovac, I don't know if I ever met him in 1991. Maybe at some meeting or other but I'm not sure that the Serb Democratic Forum even existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However, you can confirm that Mr. Pupovac and his colleagues have maintained the peaceful Serb position within Croatia and remain, in his case, an elected member of parliament today, pressing forward the principles of Serb integration and cohabitation. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right as far as Mr. Pupovac is concerned. I have to remind you that with the voice of Mr. Pupovac in the Croatian parliament, Serbs became even less than a national minority. He was saying things like, "I hope the Croat people will know how to reward this." Once Mr. Pupovac came to see me in Zagreb, but only to say that before the constitution is amended, I should say something like the Serbs were a national minority. I think he was a spy of Mr. Franjo Tudjman's. I don't even think that it is true today, because the Serbs are being harassed today as they were then. They have no human or national rights. Let Mr. Pupovac return to me and all the others their apartments and their property. Let the Croatia return that if it is really a democratic country. I haven't heard of Mr. Pupovac or Mr. Mesic advocating something like that. For instance, there is also the foreign currency savings that haven't been paid back to Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have been paid back to Croats, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Even if you don't remember going to meetings of the Serb Democratic Forum, would it be fair to say that in 1991 your affiliation moved towards Babic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as Mr. Babic is concerned, he was only on my horizon from 1993 onwards. In 1992, I still wasn't a member of any political party and there was no need for me to associate with Mr. Babic or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I must go back to one thing that I wanted you to look at. Perhaps we'll play a short extract of some speeches by Jovan Raskovic. It's part of a documentary called "Neighbours," which is an independent production. We got it from -- we've got a transcript for it, but I would be grateful again if the interpreters would -- it's Sanction as well -- if the interpreters would help us with the actual language used. And when it's going to be played, the first extract is from near Benkovac, your town, on the 17th of August. If you can play it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] We will kill Tudjman! We will kill Tudjman! "We will kill Ustashas! We will kill Ustashas! "Thank you. Thank you. Do not ask me for weapons. Do not ask weapons from me, but if weapons should be necessary, I hope somebody will be found who will give them to you. "Jovo Serb, Jovo the Serb. "It is a good thing that planes are flying above us. It is a good thing that our Yugoslav army is present. These planes that have just flown over are a message from the skies, and everybody knows that the JNA is a peaceful army, that it will not raise its sword against anyone!"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we pause there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you present at that meeting in or near your hometown on the 17th of August of 1990. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that happened on the 17th of August, 1990, the day after the police forces or, rather, members of the Zadar police station seized weapons from the reservists, from police reservists. But that very morning there was a rally before the Municipal Assembly of Benkovac where deputies in the Municipal Assembly spoke and asked for the weapons to be returned. That rally continued. And I addressed the rally and asked the people not to attack the policemen themselves for giving up the weapons in the first place. However, this rally you just showed on this video clip took place in Vukovic in late afternoon, and I attended that rally, although I didn't speak --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me finish. That rally took place that afternoon. It was organised by the Serbian Democratic Party. I was not a member of that party, but as an MP I attended the rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what we can see quite clearly is that despite the lack of pre-existing personal violence of the type I've identified, the crowd is already, responsive to Raskovic or on its own volition, shouting, "We will kill Tudjman." There was extreme language used and generated on both sides in this conflict, wasn't there, at an early stage? Or do you think those observations by the crowd were justified?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was there, please allow me to try to explain very briefly. It is true that the crowd cried and shouted, "We will kill Tudjman," but that was after the police paramilitary units were sent the night before from Korenica to act against unarmed people. And there had been a previous peaceful rally before the Municipal Assembly of Benkovac. This crowd shouted out of fear, after those police forces had been sent from Benkovac -- sorry, from Korenica to Benkovac. And they were afraid. Those were unarmed people. The same shouts could be heard in the Bukovic village. You have to know that around 3.00 three helicopters were sent against those people. It was an armed attack. And you know that the army did not take any action, even after that meeting where Raskovic spoke. As an MP I was interested and I couldn't be everywhere at the same time, but from where I had been I think I was able to assess the situation quite objectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, did you join in these chants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why was it so easy for you to resist that sort of -- why was it so easy for you to resist that sort of behaviour and yet the vast majority of the crowd seemed to be engaging in that sort of behaviour? What distinguishes you from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will tell you, Mr. Bonomy. It wasn't easy even for me. I must tell you that I was -- I had never been afraid in my life as I was afraid then, but can you imagine those people? Their level of educational attainment isn't that high. The police had been sent to kill them all. And I can understand those chants on their part. In addition to that, in 1990, I think it was March, the HDZ was set up in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me of the basis on which you say the police had been sent to kill them all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the basis is the later development of events that made it clear: An assault against Serbs to serve as an alibi for secession from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we're at the 17th of August. There's been one murder, according to you. There's been the removal of arms from the police. That's not a basis for saying, "The police are coming to kill us all." So what is it these people are really demonstrating about and what has caused it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What caused it are earlier events in the pre-election campaign and elections, but also what happened on the previous day when the MUP of Croatia sent three vehicles full of armed men, and the people were informed about it the next morning. And this crowd is responding to that. They see it as struggling for survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that Knin was cut off from Croatia as of the 17th of August? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to Exhibit 352, tab 36. Again, you'll understand I'm doing things chronologically and for a purpose. This is a document that we looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should have asked: Can that last clip please be admitted? The witness says he was present at the rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 953, along with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document, I imagine you'll be familiar with it in some way or other. It's dated the 1st of April, 1991. So back in 1991. And it's a decision on the joining of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina to the Republic of Serbia. Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina joins itself to the Republic of Serbia. "By this decision's entry into force, the territory of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina becomes a constituent part of the unified state territory of the Republic of Serbia." Now, your regions were part of Croatia. Do you believe you had any constitutional right suddenly to declare yourselves part of another state?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this decision, I haven't seen it before, but I know this: It's the 1st of April, 1991, as it says here, however, already back in 1990, the Croatian Assembly passed a decision separating the Republic of Croatia from Yugoslavia, and the Serbian Democratic Party followed up by exercising that same right on behalf of the Serbian people who were entitled to join others. Just as the Croats had that right, Serbs had the same entitlement, according to the constitution. That is not in dispute. But since I didn't follow these decisions, I was not really organised into those parliaments or districts or whatever they were called, but I believe that later, as far as I remember, although I can't be sure, this decision was made null and void or it wasn't approved or something. But according to the constitution, the Serbian people in Croatia had the same rights as the Croat people. The Serbian Democratic Party organised itself to follow up --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the actions of the Croatian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If there is a constitutional law issue that arises of significance it will be dealt with, of course, by others and not you because you're not a lawyer and I'm not asking you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have a look at the question you asked, though, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I said did he believe personally and he's given his expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I now come to the next point, which is perhaps more substantial, and it's this: Isn't it clear that before any eruption of real violence, because this is the 1st of April, the Serbs in Croatia have gone through the process of seeking effectively ethnic separation by the declaration of the RSK, and they've already sought to join Serbia before the eruption of any real interpersonal violence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as the rights of both sides go, I'm not lawyer myself, but as Mr. Bonomy said, I can say that that right is something that is enjoyed equally by both Serbs and Croats. Now, what you say before 1991 or, rather, in 1990 as well, that there had been no violence, is not true, because in 1991, we had violence throughout Croatia already. We had Opacic, Ogulin, Zagreb, Gospic, the Drava and Sava rivers, Western Slavonia, et cetera. So these processes had already been started. Now, as far as the Republic of Srpska Krajina was concerned, it just followed the proceedings in the Croatian parliament. Everything the Croatian parliament did with respect to rights and forceful secession from Yugoslavia, the Serbian Democratic Party, which was organised in -- availed itself of that same right that was accorded to the Serb people pursuant to the constitution, and you see that the Republic of Srpska Krajina in fact lagged behind those events because, if I have to remind you of this, that in October already we had -- in 1990, that is, or, rather, 1991, October, the government of the Republic of Croatia had already proclaimed that the army was illegal on the territory on Croatia. Terrible things, in a legal state. I ask you, if that had taken place in your country, what would your countrymen have done? What would their reaction have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was following this particular decision that we have the most famous opening incidents of violence; Borovo Selo, Pakrac, and at about the same time Plitvice. I may have time to go back to look at the detail of those, but do you accept that those are the events May -- April, May of 1991, they were the first incidents of significant interpersonal violence on your territory?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know events about Borovo Selo and that area, but although Plitvice is outside my own constituency, I think that Plitvice, that the situation there's quite clear: The Croatian paramilitaries stormed the area and launched an onslaught on the people and property in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to accept that and I'm not in a position to go into it in the time available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is your case, that the first incidents of violence started in August or in April, May? Because earlier you'd put August, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I said August -- no, it's April. It's in March, April, May. Plitvice, Pakrac, and Borovo Selo. Pakrac on the 1st and Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we move on in time, you mentioned Kijevo, I think. What can you say about Kijevo in a sentence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know much, but I do know that the police forces stationed in the village of Kijevo -- rather, the MUP of Croatia opened a new police station there, and I know that the surrounding Serb inhabitants were there and this was an attempt to provoke them. Now, what happened later and how Croatia was separated from Yugoslavia has become common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kijevo was a critical place for communication, wasn't it? It's an important road.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the village very well, but I assume there is something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to that extent, as we're going to discover, it matches in the interests of the RSK the position of Skabrnja, which is also on a critical road. Do you accept that? Critical line of communication.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim 100 per cent, but I don't think so. Skabrnja is a bordering village between the -- the municipality of Benkovac and Zadar. And on the other side, towards Zadar, you have Croatian territories, whereas on the other side, towards the Benkovac municipality, you have Serb territory. I don't know that Kijevo was in that same situation or, rather, perhaps I don't know the villages well enough, but I don't think so. It's this borderline where on the one side you have ethnic Croats and the other side ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at a second clip, again from "The Death of Yugoslavia," but with two people talking about what happened at Kijevo. And again I'm interested in the exact language of Mladic and Martic. We'll distribute the transcripts that we have. And this is Sanction as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] In the service of the homeland of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with my brother officers and I --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The verb was lost.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] In the service of the fatherland of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with my brother officers and everybody from all the nations and nationalities and with my units. "The Croats didn't find the colonel as evenhanded as he claimed when he --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is once again the same thing, an incorrect translation, which we see in the written translation of the English. He says that he is serving his country - I'm paraphrasing him now - with his comrades from amongst the ranks of all the nations and nationalities, and he's saying that he is serving his country with his comrades from the ranks of all the nations and nationalities. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whereas the translation here was he was that he was protecting or defending, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, pay more attention to the -- to the actual interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Press on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Kijevo is Croatian but it -- behind the village were Serb villages which were blocked. The Croats did not allow through Kijevo that any supplies should reach those Serb villages. When I decided to make an ultimatum, put an ultimatum to Kijevo -- "To the Kijevo police, who were Croats like the rest of the villagers. It demanded that the police quit their post. When they refused, Colonel Mladic ordered the regular Yugoslav army into action. It was the first time they had brazenly fought for the Serb cause. They pounded the Croatians into submission. "[Interpretation] In Kijevo, every house was fired on with all -- all weapons of the unit. We did not destroy a single house simply for the sake of it. "[In English] Once the army was done, the local Serbs walked in. "[Interpretation] I think that we were far superior to the Croats. Of course a few houses in that clash was set fire to as things go, by the artillery. "[In English] The Yugoslav flag was raised as the army seized Croat town after Croat --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forget the commentary. I'm not interested in the commentary. Just listening to the words of Mladic and Martic, is it right as we look at the development of things in your part of Croatia, is it right that Kijevo was an all-out attack involving Mladic and Martic on a small village? Is that your understanding of the position?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what year that was. Can you tell me, please, what year? I can't remember when this took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kijevo was August 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you repeat the question again, please? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Is it right that in your part of Croatia Kijevo was the first instance of an all-out attack involving both Mladic and Martic on a small village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that Mladic took part. We saw the footage. But I do know that as far as Kijevo is concerned, every inhabitant was really armed, and I knew that humanitarian -- I know that humanitarian aid couldn't be driven through the village. It was 1995, and that there were Croatian paramilitaries stationed there. It wasn't the regular police. They were the "Redarstvenici," as they were called. And as far as I remember from the press, the president of the municipality, or the Executive Council perhaps, I think his surname was Betal [phoen], Veljko Popovic was provoked when he passed through and tried to calm the situation down. I think he was attacked, along with somebody else whose surname I can't remember now. It's not the Croatian police force here. It was illegal police forces which were not within the police system that had come to block the passage through the village, as far as I remember. I think that's what happened. The irregular police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript refers to 1995, but you're talking about 1991, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are talking about 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Still staying with 1991, can we look at -- 643, tab 4. Trying to get the development of things in your area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just before you leave that. How do we know -- or are you suggesting that that filming was done at the time of the action or is that just odd film to illustrate the commentary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course my understanding is that the film relates to the time of the action indeed. I'm principally interested in the words of the actors Mladic and Martic. And I would ask for that clip to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 954.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look now please at this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Without the transcript because these transcripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The transcripts are not very helpful so without the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document that you have. It's already an exhibit, 643, tab 4. You can see that it's a source of military information from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, Milorad Boskovic, and it deals with somebody called Captain Dragan, also known by his name of Daniel Snedden, and it explains, if we would be good enough, please, Mr. Nort, to go to the second page, about how this man had come to the Krajina - second page - and had indeed operated as a trainer, as an instructor. Do you know anything about Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. I really don't. His activities are not something that is known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard of him from the press, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did he have a training camp near your area or indeed in your area?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his training camp, but from the press I learnt that he did have some training camp somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in your area, in the Krajina there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From reading about it in the papers, it said that he was training volunteers somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just go back to the first page, Mr. Nort. We'll see that it refers to: "By mid-June security organs gathered the initial information on Captain Dragan engaged in the training of the special unit of the SAO Krajina in the village of Golubic near Knin." Does that ring any bells for you? Golubic would be about, I suppose, 50 kilometres, as the crow flies, from Benkovac in a north-easterly direction or in an easterly direction, wouldn't it? Did you know about his training camps?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I was never in Golubic nor did I pass through it. I know that it's on the territory of Knin municipality, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the establishment of the Red Berets in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about their establishment but I had heard of the existence of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the year. I can't remember the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, given your position as a politician, to see matters that you may know a little more about. Do you remember that it was on the 17th of August, oddly enough, a year after the log revolution, the 17th of August of 1991, that something called the Belgrade Initiative was launched? Do you remember that initiative?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case we'll move on to The Hague conference. Were you aware of The Hague conference starting in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I didn't follow the activities of The Hague conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not at all, even as a person interested in politics locally?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I read something about it at the time, but I don't know what you're referring to now. Remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the conference lasted some time and offered confederation and was refused by this accused. Were you aware of none of that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While I was going to come to it later, since you asked me, I'll just help you with this: Were you aware that in the course of The Hague conference, or in its development, consideration was or would have been given to giving your parts of Croatia something called special status with a very high level of autonomy for the Serbs? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was The Hague conference or not, but everything that the international community, and in this case I don't know about The Hague community -- conference, whether it was the European Community or not, they were not legal matters. The international community as me, Atlagic, in 1995 protected me from the paramilitaries, but it brought me -- well, you see where; here and in Belgrade. So that was all -- it wasn't the Croats that forced me out. It was the international community. That was my legal protector in 1995, whereas it cleansed me, along with 500.000 other inhabitants of the Serb area of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the most important thing, Mr. Nice, would be -- the most important thing is that Dr. Franjo Tudjman already in 1990 accepted to talk to the deputies - that would have been the most important thing, had he accepted to talk to them - where there were Serb members. He never wanted that. I was the initiator, but he didn't accept my offer. The only person who wished to talk and negotiate was Dr. Vlado Vasenica [phoen] from a party whose name I can't remember now, but he wasn't even allowed to come into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't allow him, the HDZ and paramilitaries didn't allow him to come into the area to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It sounds as though you're saying that you were completely unaware that consideration was given to your areas having special highly autonomous status within Croatia if The Hague proposals had been accepted. Were you completely unaware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I have forgotten what all that was about. But I do know that the Serbs in Krajina at that time followed in the steps of what the Croats were doing. When the Croats did something, they did something; when the Croats seceded from Yugoslavia, then Republika Srpska Krajina seceded from Croatia, pursuant to the same constitution that was in force. So they sought the same rights as the Croatians enjoyed. That's the only thing I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I want to explore with you is this: Before those proposals, as I must suggest to you, were rejected, we should deal with developing violence in your area. Let's look at this map, which is part of Exhibit 336, just to remind ourselves of where everything is. We can see Benkovac. I've highlighted a few areas. We can see Benkovac. Then to the east we can see Golubic, where the training camp I suggested was. And then between Benkovac and Zadar we can see Skabrnja and Nadin. Skabrnja, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Nadin. And it's clear, isn't it, that Skabrnja lies between a railway line and a major road into Zadar. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Skabrnja is along the railway line, in fact, between Benkovac and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you offered some --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a village, and there's a train station in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You offered some information on the basis of a source of information who spoke to you - don't name him - some time ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wanted to express personal concern about the use of time, because we did make an order about how time should be divided, and for various reasons which we don't need to explore at the moment, that order is not being adhered to as far as the Prosecution is concerned. I quite accept that it's not a mandatory or obligatory order in the sense of others that the Trial Chamber issues, but if this practice continues, then there's no way it's ever going to be met within the time scale allocated for the Defence case, and I'm concerned that you do not appear to be taking any steps to try to bring your use of time within that time scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm making every effort I can. When witnesses come and give wide-ranging evidence, it's, if I may say so, easier said than done, to apply the test to ourselves, simply to select those items that will fit the allotted amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I understand that, but -- and I understand also that it's a legitimate exercise of cross-examination to expand the Prosecution case, but what we're trying to do is be fair in the allocation of time, and you had your opportunity to present the Prosecution case, and it may be that continuing to do that rather than to challenge what's being presented by the Defence is what's causing this. And while, as again I emphasise, it's a legitimate thing to do, in the overall context of the timing in this case, it may not be the appropriate way to proceed in fairness to everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's concern. Can I answer it in this way: What I've been doing this morning is in fact challenging his evidence, because the evidence given is of two types, specific where he's dealt usually by hearsay with particular events, but also general and specific where he's dealt with themes. And to challenge those themes - if Your Honour will indulge me - to challenge those themes and to show that they are false and therefore to put the Prosecution's case, which is my other duty, I'm afraid sometimes needs an exploration of matters from many areas. I'm quite -- I hope to finish by the end of this morning's session for a range of reasons, and I may decide to go almost no further after the session when I've summarised things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you don't misunderstand my position, Mr. Nice, I fully appreciate that in relation to every witness you could make exactly the same point as you've just made. That doesn't deal with the overall issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point is there was to be an overall use of time and now that you've got into this predicament, I would suggest something has to be done to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing that I can do to resolve it -- take this witness. I don't know that the witness needs to be in here while we discuss it, but I don't mind his being here. I could, I suppose, have simply taken the one or two pieces of evidence that might have seemed to be concrete, Skabrnja and Bruska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not dealing with my point, because I accept all that. I think there is no answer to the point except for you to review your position, and I'm simply encouraging you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked for the witness to be kept out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We are going to move on, Mr. Nice, with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I was only going to seek your assistance but I can do it in the presence of the witness, or I can do it after the witness is concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we return briefly to private session to conclude what I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One point that I omitted to get correct is that even if he'd started or was at sometime at Golubic, the man Dragan's camp was actually at Bruska, very near to Benkovac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bruska is near Benkovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he had his camp there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had it in Golubic or there. I really don't know anything about the activities of that man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, were you living in Benkovac at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the time from 1990 to 1995, I lived in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you didn't know about these activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't, but I heard the name of Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, please, and I'm now going to turn very rapidly to Skabrnja, could we look at Exhibit 352 tab 166. Your Honours, this is a document that contained a letter from Martic with his own English version of it. It is only that English version that has been admitted. There is now another English translation but I better rely on the English version that is in evidence, and if Mr. Nort would place that on the overhead projector. Mr. Atlagic, on the 28th of September, and you've got the original, I hope, B/C/S version, and we'll put Martic's own English version on the overhead projector, Martic said on the 28th of September: "We have surely information that on the 29/30 ... of September, by force, immigration of the population is planned for Skabrnja, Novi Grad and Pridraga. In the view that the Croatian side knows very well our attitude, it means that the immigration of population confirms a special commission of the RSK Government, therefore should exist suitable conditions, we inform you that we will be forced to present by force arrival on the territory of Republic Serbian Krajina. We have opinion that the prevention of the arrival in the RSK, Croatian side will use as a motive for the offensive actions ..." So he's threatening or offering the use of force. Do you remember this incident being a forerunner to what happened at Skabrnja? Sorry, after. No, sorry, it's ... No. Very well. I'll come back to that letter because -- can I deal with Skabrnja in a different way and very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will remember or will be reminded that there are many exhibits dealing with Skabrnja and I'll list them: Exhibit 387, tab 33, Exhibit 387, tab 34; Exhibit 387, tab 35; and Exhibit 475, tab 4. Time means I'll just take tab -- Exhibit 475, tab 4, and we'll look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, there are a number of reports that are available to the Court on what happened in Skabrnja, and I'm only going to rely or refer you to one of them. So if we look at this document, you can see that it comes from Simo Rosic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but before showing me this document, you showed me another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one from Milan Martic. Can I just say that you say this preceded what happened in Skabrnja, whereas this document is dated 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we'll come back to that in a second. Please concentrate on this -- please concentrate on this document. Now, this document is an Official Note coming from Simo Rosic. It's dated the 8th of March of 1992, and it says, second paragraph -- well, he's conducted interviews with personnel, and he says: "As the collected data shows that the killings -" this is in Skabrnja and Nadin - "were committed by members of the Benkovac Territorial Defence special units, or units that fought under their command. These were volunteers from Serbia and Opacic's group composed of combatants from this area. "Volunteers from Serbia committed murder in Skabrnja village, while, according to unconfirmed data, Opacic's groups killed members of the Odzakovic family (the Boxer) in Nadin and killed three people captured from Skabrnja village in Smilcic." He then goes on to give matters of detail of something that happened in Skabrnja. Do you accept on the basis of this official report, prepared at the time by the Lieutenant Commander Rosic, that in fact the killings in Skabrnja were committed by people from Serbia in a group headed by Opacic at least in part?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this group that is referred to here, this Opacic's group, but as for the group in Serbia, I doubt it, especially since Colonel Stefanovic got killed. I don't know why a group from Serbia needed to come there if there was the Territorial Defence from Benkovac plus the army acting as a buffer. I don't believe that anybody from Serbia did these things. And as for this other group, I really don't know. Maybe somebody else knows more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We had evidence in this court which I want you to deal with in light of your account that it was all, as it were, innocent on the Serb part, from Marko Miljanic, a Croat, and he gives an account of the -- a detailed account of how the attack was mounted and spoke in terms of not only what he saw but of overhearing a conversation between Mladic and a Lieutenant Colonel Cecovic in a communications room. He overheard a radio communication. Do you know Lieutenant Colonel Cecovic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I really don't know anything about these military men as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the suggestion is, and you claim to have information of a reliable kind coming from this area close to your town, the information is that there was the sound of an ammunition truck or something exploding. Cecovic proposed withdrawal and Mladic told him that if he withdrew he'd shoot him, and he stayed on. The evidence goes on to speak about helicopters arriving. That's the evidence before this Court. Did you know anything about a loud explosion? It's in your area. Did you know anything about helicopters arriving with troops that then entered Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I'm hearing it for the first time now from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, that evidence was given in this court by an eyewitness. He didn't know what other evidence there might be. We've now had evidence in things called Supreme Defence Council records. I haven't got the time to go to them, but one of them shows that the man Cecovic was rewarded by promotion, inter alia, for preserving the western borders of the RSK. In seizing Skabrnja which lay between the railway line and an important road, what he was doing was preserving the -- the western borders, wasn't he? That would be a proper interpretation of what you're doing. You're preserving the western borders by taking Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You should link up these events in a slightly broader context. Before Skabrnja, again in November, you have the expulsion of Serbs from Western Slavonia. The same things are happening at the same time. Skabrnja is coordinated with Western Slavonia because Croatian forces attacked Serbs in Western Slavonia. They're doing the same thing in November in Skabrnja. And already on the 16th of November -- sorry, 16th of October, 1991, the government had by that time already ordered the army to withdraw, and immediately afterwards these attacks on Serbs followed. The order had been given on the 16th October, 1991, to the army to withdraw, and at that time the army was already under attack in all areas of Croatia, especially barracks. You didn't allow me to tell you this yesterday, but Spegelj is now saying himself that the attacks on barracks were carried out on his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you've answered my question but I'm going to move on to this: First of all, the man Cecovic, who you say you don't know, was actually the commander of the Benkovac Brigade. Are you sure you didn't know this man, if you were there and a politician in a town of the size of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be specific and answer you truthfully. I don't know this man. And you keep emphasising that I was a politician. I was just a representative who by that time was not even recognised by the Croatian authorities. You know how much politicians can do when conflicts have already started. I was not even a politician of the Serbian Democratic Party and did not engage in their activities, so I was not in a position to know all these things --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that were organised by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... extract was drawn is 666, tab 37, the minute of the 13th of June of 1995. Further, in relation to Skabrnja, again given in live evidence without necessarily access to these documents, the witness Milan Babic explained that the man -- he had heard that the man Goran Klempo Opacic had been involved in the killings, and he also explained that General Vukovic had told him that this village had to be taken before the winter so that he could make the lines, that's the lines of the Yugoslav People's Army's occupation, straight, and that the Croat villages disturbed -- of Skabrnja and Nadin disturbed that line. Now, that's in material before this Court. Thinking back and remembering how much you actually did know or you did experience, or how little, isn't the truth that Skabrnja and Nadin were taken for specifically territorial reasons?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Nobody intended to take Skabrnja or Nadin. The case is that Croatian paramilitary formations staged daily provocations against Serb population. You know that Skabrnja happened in November, whereas before that, the 16th of October, 1991, the Croatian government issued an order that the army should withdraw from Croatian territory, and attacks started immediately against the army. Two soldiers were killed very early on. You are trying to represent these incidents as something organised by the local people and incursions from people from Serbia. You have heard the testimony of Mr. Mesic here. Everybody knows what was done by those people who were trying to break up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To finish this point and to try to come to a rapid end, the man Opacic, known as Klempo, was honoured and rewarded as a Red Beret in a ceremony in 1997 - we don't have time to look at it in detail - for his work in this area, and I am suggesting to you that the man Opacic was rewarded for his work in the Supreme defence Council. We've seen what is said about Martic's connection outside the area. Isn't the reality that something like the taking of Skabrnja was put in place by people including people from Serbia or from outside the area and probably directed from outside the area? Looking back, isn't that the truth? I got the names wrong. Yes. It was Cecovic who was rewarded in the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not true. Skabrnja would never have been taken, and Serbs never took anything or launched aggression against anything. They just defended their homes and fields. And if you talk about Skabrnja, nobody attacked that place until the situation in Serb villages close to Skabrnja became unbearable because of daily attacks. And you have this decision of the Croatian government of the 16th of October, 1991, that the army must withdraw by November, and the army from that time on was constantly under attack in all areas of Croatia. And I'm not aware of this man being decorated in 1995. I really don't know about it. And if you are talking about the evidence of a particular witness that you heard here, these witnesses have a particular relationship to those persons, so you can't trust them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of your exhibits, tab 13, please, I suggested at an earlier stage that the Chamber might have found this an interesting document to read and I don't know if it took up my invitation. You will have heard me express my concerns yesterday about extracts being taken from documents, and let my make it quite plain, although my objection to extracts being used doesn't necessarily mean I suggest the authors are unreliable, for example, I'm just informing the Court really, through you, the man Puhovski is a man who features in human rights reports on which we might well rely if we had time. But this one, Exhibit tab 13, is we've got in context. We looked at only the first two sentences, but if we look at the rest of it, under the heading "Can geese save the city?" I want your comments on some of the things he says. He speaks of intellectuals, and this is in December 1991 -- put it on the overhead projector, bottom of the page: "Serbian and Croatian nationalism were considered to be dangerous while, for example, the ethnic sentiments of Macedonians and Muslims were flattered. All this was subordinate to the principles of the communist dictatorship. The roots of this dictatorship were deeper here than elsewhere, because the communist system was not introduced to Yugoslavia at the end of foreign bayonets. The Yugoslav revolution had its own social and national sources, and Tito was its genuine hero. The dispute over the responsibility for Titoism has continued to the present day. The Serbs claim that they suffered discrimination in the Yugoslavia run by the communists. The Croats claim that Yugoslavia was simply a different version of Serbian domination over other nations. And both are right to an extent. This is how they accept reality and consciousness about reality as an important part of the same reality." And then this about this accused: "This is not the place to explain the unusually complex Serbo-Albanian dispute over Kosovo. Let us say only this: Slobodan Milosevic, the Communist leader of Serbia, has succeeded in winning over a large swathe of public opinion with the slogan of defending the Serbs in Kosovo." Now, this is a Polish intellectual of great repute writing at the end of 1991. So at that stage development of violence was limited. Do you agree with him that by the end of 1991 this accused had won over swathes of public opinion with the slogan of "defending the Serbs in Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we talk about the accused, Slobodan Milosevic, he did not win anybody over. There is a large number of Serb people standing behind him to this day. I don't know what the purpose of this reading is at all. If you take the Serbian approach to Kosovo, you are not going to tell me, are you, that Kosovo doesn't belong to Serbia. It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same thing as asking you whether England is part of some other territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The paragraph continues about defending the historic tradition of Serbia, seeing a natural ally in this accused, and yet he was -- same page -- he was also supported by the intellectuals who for years fought with the Communist apparatus. "They believed that Milosevic would destroy communism by giving back the Serbs their identity, and that they would be his intellectual and executive apparatus. This alliance was an illusion about the road to broad support, an illusion about the road to power, one to which intellectuals frequently succumb in their belief that their ideas will become a material force at the moment the masses accept them." And he goes on, and this is the last part I want, although I'd like the Chamber to read the whole of the document: "Milosevic was the embodiment of a variant of national communism familiar in other countries too. In Romania those ideas were represented by Ceaucescu, in Poland by Moczar, although Milosevic was a far more intellectual and skilful incarnation. He used this to conquer the Serbs and seduce a number of intellectuals."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your question in relation to this, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this witness agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't agree with this passage. You cannot compare Milosevic to Ceaucescu or Yugoslavia to Romania. This is child talk. Serbia has its own specific road, and if you talk about President Milosevic, he was in favour of Yugoslavia as a federal state based on equality of all peoples. Everybody knows that. If you are going to claim that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he broke up Yugoslavia, those who broke up Yugoslavia sat in my witness box at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On a matter that was dealt with in private session yesterday, very briefly in private session today, and then I shall try and be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not -- I simply don't have time to do more than to note that in the document I showed earlier to this witness, the Martic letter of September 28th --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that the letter we were looking at first - I got it out of order - shows the reaction of Martic to the possible repopulation of this area by Croats. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not my understanding of it. I don't understand it like you do, Mr. Nice. It says reliable information that in 1992, et cetera, et cetera, that forcible repopulation of the area in Skabrnja, et cetera, et cetera. But listen, this is 1992 now. We're talking about 1992 now, and the events took place in 1991. So that it is highly unpopular later on to re-populate the border belt by anyone, because there is the threat to the population there, anybody coming up to the front line. Of course, I'm not a military expert myself, but I'm following logics here. And I don't think Martic ever strove for the forcible repopulation of or re-establishment of any population. At least, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
