utterances.text: And then finally, because you remained a politician, you remained in Benkovac right through from The Hague conference through the various other negotiations that you may have heard about, through the Vance Plan, the Cutileiro Plan, the Washington Agreement, the Contact Group plan -- well, that's for Bosnia -- the Z-4 plan for Croatia, we will explore this maybe with other witnesses but I want your comment on this: All international proposals that were made were one way or another rejected by the Serbs in Croatia for whom they were in part aimed to benefit. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. Not all the proposals were rejected by the Serbs. For example, I'm not aware of although I don't know about this later period that much, but I don't know that the last agreement was rejected by the Serbs in Croatia because the -- it was Mr. Babic who signed the agreement, the Z-4 agreement. Mr. Babic signed it before the exodus took place. However that agreement, the Z-4 agreement, regardless of the fact that Babic signed it, the Croatian Sabor or parliament never adopted it. Croatia did not wish to have any Z-4 agreement. So when we're looking at this, you must look at it in relation to the Croatian government and the steps it took when it came to politics, regardless of whether -- what the Serbs did. Well, in 1990 the Serbs offered autonomy. Raskovic was a Serb. The Croatian authorities did not accept that, and Babic is somebody who you've been referring to for the past two days and he was the one who signed the Z-4 plan. The greatest exodus in history in the past 200 years took place, and as a representative of the international community I would like to see you strive for the population going back to their territory. I'd like to go back to my own apartment, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question to you is this: The truth that is your evidence and your behaviour at the time was motivated by overwhelming desire, without violence driving it, for separation from the Croats and indeed for joining to Serbia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose statement, Mr. Nice? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give an example of the behaviour of this witness that you're relying on as a foundation for that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, let me make it quite plain to you, Mr. Atlagic, your evidence insofar as it seeks to exculpate the Serbs at every turn is evidence, I must suggest to you, is coloured and not accurate. You've given evidence that is exculpatory of the Serbs: No offences committed by them, innocent at Skabrnja, innocent at Bruska, and I suggest to you that that evidence is coloured and not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Nice, you're not dealing with my point when you say that. I'm asking you if there's an evidential foundation for saying that this witness's behaviour - and by that you're not referring to his evidence, because you dealt with that separately - his behaviour indicated that he wanted the objective that you refer to; separation from the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case I must withdraw the word "behaviour," and it's his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was, I think, what I intended and I don't -- I don't -- I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there isn't any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are a very strange man because you're insinuating that I said something I didn't and that doesn't stem from my testimony and evidence. Now, as far as my behaviour is concerned and I myself was concerned, I am an honourable man, a decent man, and that is how I behave towards both the Croats and the Serbs. And the Croats know that full well, and I'm very pleased to say -- see that they are attending these proceedings, so don't insinuate anything. Now, as far as the Serb responsibility is concerned, I didn't say that there were no -- there was no individual responsibility when it comes to crimes, but you cannot justify a state which was formed on the basis of crimes against the Serb people. How are you going to justify that because it was violent in your position as Prosecutor? Listen here, Mr. Nice, we are -- you're attempting to try Mr. Milosevic here and you are trying me here, you're trying yourself here, and the Trial Chamber, the Court here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since you asked those questions, you have described this Court as a monster Court and your favoured politician of all is still Vojislav Seselj, isn't he? You believe him to be a great adornment.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not describe him that way. Don't insinuate something that you wish to hear from me. That is not what I said. I didn't say he was monstrous. When it comes to the Court, I have my opinion and you know what my opinion is, but don't link up Vojislav Seselj in this context. When it comes to Vojislav Seselj, I speak about him with pride. I don't know why you are linking me with Vojislav Seselj at all. He's an honourable, decent man, democratically prone, Europeanly -- prone for Europe and civilisational trends and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I take it you have concluded. Yes. Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I told you yesterday that I didn't feel well, and you refused to accept that. Let me repeat: I do not feel well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, how can you say I refused to accept that? There is absolutely no basis for that. I gave specific instructions to the Court deputy and the Registrar to see that you would be examined yesterday afternoon. It's an absolute falsehood to say that I did not accept that you are not well. What is your position now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same as yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you in a position to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is one matter I'd like to ask about which I hope the witness can deal with. I'm not sure that he can, but it may be of importance. I'll try and find the reference. Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were referred to a document from the Prosecution exhibits which originated from Milan Babic, and it concerned his decision that the RSK should declare themselves as a part of Serbia on the 1st of April of 1991. That was an exhibit at 352 of the Prosecution collection, tab 36. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You referred to it as having been ruled null and void. Are you able to give any more details about the rejection of that declaration as to what party rejected it and when?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't do that now. If you were to give me more time, then I'd look into it. That wouldn't be the problem. I seem to remember hazily that somebody did reject it, not only reject it in Krajina but I think in Serbia as well. So it never took effect, and the events that followed speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You were a politician there at the time. Were you aware of the declaration by Milan Babic that the RSK would be a part of Serbia from the 1st of April? Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't aware of that, but I know it on the basis of some general events, that there were rumours going round among the ordinary folk. But I didn't know the specific move. But there was always mention made that Krajina would be Krajina but within the composition of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You referred to it being rejected. Are you able to give any information about the rejection from Serbia of that declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, there was never any mention in Serbia about that, this joining. None of the officials talked about that, and not the citizens, certainly, that Krajina would be a part of Serbia, so I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's being put to you, you see, that this was a step, part of a series of steps that were being taken by the Serbian government to annex or otherwise take control of the Krajina. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as you were aware from your role in politics, was that the motivation that was coming from Serbia? Was that what the Serbian government was directing to you or your party?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, the Serb government from Belgrade nor my party was doing that. The Government of Republika Srpska Krajina, starting with the 1990s when the municipalities were established, was constituted itself, and it had a political party, the Serbian Democratic Party, which never allowed anybody to become involved from outside. The late Raskovic would not have allowed Serbia to get involved, or even Mr. Milosevic to get involved, never. And I think that is common knowledge to one and all. So I don't believe in this. Now, whether the decision was passed or not, I really can't say. I have my doubts about this piece of paper because it wasn't the wish of the people. The wish of the people was to defend themselves but it wasn't Serbia's desire, on an official level or unofficial level, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just dealing with some other -- other matters. November 1991, you were still officially a deputy of the Croatian Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said November 1991. I don't think so, not in November. Officially I was, yes, but there was an interruption in communications, so physically I wasn't able to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I put to you, that officially you were, but were you able to take part in any of the activities of the Sabor at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my activities were linked to my evidence yesterday and statements yesterday, but many others that you didn't have a chance of hearing. But later on the Croatian government never sent me any material or documents for the sessions, because they saw me as a liability because I asked the right questions in the right place. But I wasn't allowed to say yesterday, the Prosecution didn't permit me to say, it went on to other things, but I was physically attacked in the Croatian parliament. I was physically attacked in the Sabor by the deputies, and I went home, I sent in a letter of protest, because I asked that the government of Croatia take responsibility for what had happened on the ground, and I put it -- wanted to put it on the agenda. Three men came up to me and swore at me, saying that I was a Chetnik, that I went to Belgrade, and so on and so forth, and that I had nothing to do there, it wasn't my place to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That was a bit off course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In November 1991, what was your connection with the region of Skabrnja or the area, the village of Skabrnja, the area around there? Were you in the location at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I wasn't in the location, not in Skabrnja, no. It's a different municipality, and that's where the separation line was. So it was very difficult to be there up at the line, and I had no need to go there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How far away at that time were you from Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Benkovac, Skabrnja, that's a distance of not more than 15 to 20 [Realtime transcript read in error"50"] kilometres. But I was even closer. For example, I passed through the village of Biljana, which was shelled almost on a daily basis. It was shelled every day, and that's a regional road running from Benkovac to Biljana and Zadar. Benkovac, Biljana and Zemunik, that's another Serb place. So the cars were targeted all the time, so I was close by but not that close.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But were you in a position in November 1991 to have been close enough to Skabrnja to be able to understand what was happening around that village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in Biljana Donja. That's the closest point. I passed through that area. And I went to see some local municipal officials that I happened to know from earlier on, because I was president of Benkovac municipality earlier on in the 1980s, and it's not that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Atlagic, that concludes your evidence, and we thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 64, as I have it, line 2, it says no more than 50 kilometres. I think he said 15, and in any event the map shows it's 15. He said 15 to 20, according to Ms. Tromp, who was -- Yes, so 50 is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 50 is wrong. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's clearly wrong. It's 15 to 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next witness comes in, I don't know whether the Chamber would find it helpful to discuss further the time problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to hear any submissions on that now. The Chamber will consider that matter and, if necessary, invite submissions. Mr. Kay, are you in a position to lead the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Perhaps if we took the break now, because we're nearly at that stage, maybe to half past, just to see how things develop until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I inquire whether you are in a position to continue now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I certainly intend to examine my witness. Nobody else can do it. Therefore, if you feel that we must go on now, I will examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. We will continue. Just to rehearse what happened: Your earlier statement that I did not take account of your illness yesterday I consider to be demonstrably and mischievously false. I ordered yesterday that you should be examined by a competent doctor. I regret that that was not done. I have to say that on the information which I now have, you will be examined today by a specialist, either at 3.30 or at 6.00 p.m. We have just about an hour to finish, so let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bissett. Please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: My name is James Bissett. I am a citizen of Canada and former Canadian ambassador to the former Yugoslavia from October of 1990 until June of 1992. I'm here on my own behalf. That is to say I'm not representing my government, and I'm not representing any organisation or group. I am here because I was asked by Mr. Milosevic's Defence to appear and give evidence on his behalf. I was -- so I've come here on my own free will and as an individual citizen of Canada now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your background, Mr. Bissett?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent 36 years in the Government of Canada as a public servant, serving in the Department of Foreign Affairs and in the immigration service. I was the head of the Canadian immigration service from 1982 to 1985. I was then appointed High Commissioner to Trinidad and Tobago in 1982 and I served there until 1985 with the Department of External Affairs. I was then brought back to Canada and exchanged to the Immigration Department, to be the head of the Canadian immigration service. I did that job for five years and then was appointed ambassador to Yugoslavia in 1990. I retired in 1992 when I left Yugoslavia, and I went to Moscow for five years as the head of an international organisation headquartered in Geneva, called the International Organisation for Migration. We were trying to help the Russians deal with large numbers of Russians who were returning to the Russian Republic after the collapse of the Soviet Union. I retired -- I left Moscow in 1997 and returned to Canada and have been retired since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, as you have said, you were ambassador to Yugoslavia. In view of the fact that you were the ambassador of a very large country who is a NATO member, how did it come about that you wish to testify on my behalf? Why?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: I wish to testify on your behalf because while I was ambassador in Yugoslavia, during those two critical years, I found that in my dealings with you you seemed to be doing everything you could do at the time to keep Yugoslavia united. And I have followed closely the events in Yugoslavia since I left, and I find it strange that the one leader of the Yugoslav Republic that wanted to keep the country together and did whatever he could when the violence started to indeed cooperate fully with the international agencies to bring peace to Yugoslavia is now -- is now the accused at the court. Your actions while I was there would have indicated that there are others who are more deeply involved trying to break up the country and who were inciting the bloodshed and violence that you were doing your best to prevent. For those reasons, I felt that the Tribunal should at least hear my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, after you were no longer the ambassador to Yugoslavia, you continued to take an interest in events there, as you yourself have said. What were the sources of your information and how did you follow the events in Yugoslavia thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I followed the events there as closely as I could by reading the newspapers, watching television, and taking a close interest in -- in the Balkans, as I always have done. I know the history well, and I followed the events there as closely as I could. I also had former diplomatic colleagues of mine that I often discussed the situation there. So basically, by reading and being alert and taking an abiding interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You personally spoke up in public and wrote about your knowledge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was shocked and, quite frankly, appalled when I heard that my country, Canada, was joining with the NATO forces in the bombing of a sovereign Yugoslavia without going anywhere near the United Nations, which was in direct violation of the UN Charter. I was also -- I could describe myself as an old Cold War warrior, a strong admirer of NATO, fully aware that it had protected all of the Western countries from possible Soviet invasion, and I was very proud of that. But I was also aware that NATO was a treaty among countries, and Canada was one of the founding countries. And Article 1 of the NATO constitution made it very clear that NATO would not use violence in the settlement of international conflicts. Indeed, Article 1 went further and said NATO would never even threaten to use the use of force, and yet in March of 1999 it began to bomb a country that was a sovereign country, that was no threat to its neighbours, that didn't possess weapons of mass destruction, and was simply doing what any other sovereign state would do in the circumstances, was trying to suppress an armed rebellion by an organisation that had the year before been described by the State Department as a terrorist organisation. I thought that the use of violence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the United States. What State Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The United States State Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: United States. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that the use of violence to settle that minor difficulty in terms of world events was an appalling act to -- at the end of the 20th century, and unfortunately meant that we would enter into the 21st with the idea that violence was still acceptable in the settlement of international disputes. For that reason I opposed the bombing and went on a speaking tour from coast-to-coast and wherever I could to speak out against it and also to write articles about the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, in the documents that I presented along with your statement, in tab 2 there is a book by the Lord Byron Foundation for Balkan Studies. I don't want to deal with it in its entirety, I only wish to ask you a few questions about your contribution. Only the article authored by you is included here. I did not seek to tender the other parts of the book. Is this your article, Mr. Bissett?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The article entitled "New Diplomacy, Old Agenda."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll put only a few questions to you in connection with what you wrote here. You said in the first paragraph of your article: "[In English] There were a number of reasons why Yugoslavia was torn apart, but one of the primary causes of the tragedy were the failure of Western diplomacy." [Interpretation] Why did you write this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Because it is my belief that that was one of the primary causes of the tragedy. When Croatia and Slovenia had expressed their wishes to separate from Yugoslavia, there was still ample time for the Western European countries, the European Community, to step in and ensure that if the people in those countries wished to secede, that they do so in a peaceful manner and in a manner that would do justice to the other part of the equation, which was the remaining part of Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, that did not happen, and it wasn't until Slovenia used violence to seize the custom posts along the Austrian border that the federal government of Yugoslavia ordered the Yugoslav national army to go into Slovenia and restore order. Unexpectedly, the Slovenes put up a fight and the war, as we know, spilled over into Croatia and the violence continued. It seemed to me that there was many times before the actual violence occurred where the European Community could have mediated this dispute and, with its influence, urged the leaders of Croatia and Slovenia to arrange to secede within the constitution and in a lawful manner without using violence. They failed to do that. In addition to that, some members of the European Community - and I will name them: Germany in the forefront - I think it's clear encouraged and supported the separation of Slovenia and Croatia. We know that arms were being shipped into Croatia and Slovenia from some of the central European powers, Hungary, for example, and armed militia was being formed in those countries. There was ample notice to the international community that trouble was brewing in Yugoslavia, but nothing was done to try and prevent the violence from spreading or to mediate the dispute until it was too late. So that's why I describe it as a failure of Western diplomacy. I might amplify on that. I think part of the problem was that these were -- these were events that were taking place in the shadow of the Maastricht Treaty, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the fall of the Berlin Wall, and countries were preoccupied with other things and were ignoring Yugoslavia and the events that were taking place there. That's one part of it. The other, however, was I think a deliberate attempt on the part of Germany to encourage separation of Croatia and Slovenia. I call that a failure of diplomacy because I believe there was time, and there could have been interest in trying to ensure that the break-up of Yugoslavia, if it was to occur, could have been done with peace and, as I said, in a lawful fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bissett, and we would be grateful if your answers could be shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To go a step further, Mr. Bissett, in the third paragraph of your article, speaking of Yugoslavia, you say: "[In English] The ethnic differences have been frequently exploited by outside powers and used by them to divide the nation and tear it apart with ethnic hatred and violence." [Interpretation] Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I put that in the content of the history of the Balkans. The history of the Balkans has always shown that when outside powers intervene, the local inhabitants become involved in the struggle and it results in religious and ethnic violence. This is not something new in the Balkans. It's been going on for many centuries. The Ottomans, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, the Nazis in the Second World War, the communists after the war, and more recently, NATO's involvement in Yugoslavia. These foreign powers often intervene there for -- not with any interest in what local problems are but with an effort to try and satisfy their own foreign policy objectives by involving themselves in the Balkan politics. It's been going on for many, many years, and it's just too bad that it occurred again in the 1990s. So that's what I mean, the history shows that outside interference often --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's enough for the history and background. You should now lead the witness to evidence that's more directly related to the period under consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, on page 2 in the third paragraph from the bottom, you mention the premature recognition of Slovenia and Croatia by the European Union. I hope you can find that passage. "[In English] The premature recognition of Slovenia and Croatia by the European Union ..." You can read it out yourself. Please read it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: I can't find it. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Number four, fourth paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The premature recognition of Slovenia and Croatia by the European Union, extended under intense German pressure in Maastricht in 1991, was a guarantee that the break-up of Yugoslavia would not be resolved by peaceful means. Once again, Western intervention had exacerbated and complicated a serious Balkan problem." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before you reply, the time you are referring to is the time when you yourself were in Yugoslavia at the heart of these events, because you were the Canadian ambassador to Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: That is correct. What I mean by that passage is that the German insistence on recognising the independence of Slovenia and Croatia was premature because once Croatia and Slovenia had gained recognition, of course they lost any interest in sitting down and negotiating with other parties about the separation. It had become a fait accompli. Therefore, there was no interest in their leaders of getting back around the bargaining table to try and resolve the violence that was occurring, settle the national debt, the sharing of property, and all of those things that happen when a country separates from a union. I'm not the only one who has considered that Germany's pressure on the European Community for premature recognition was a guarantee that violence and bloodshed would continue in Yugoslavia. There are a lot of other observers who have made that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, you arrived in Yugoslavia when it was already in crisis. According to your experience and knowledge, what were the key elements of that crisis?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I think the crisis was that it was very clear that Yugoslavia was breaking apart and that Slovenia, certainly Croatia, possibly Bosnia, were aspiring for -- to break apart and form independent countries. That was -- that was the crisis. Following that, the additional crisis was that there was the potential for dreadful violence to take place, because in all of the republics paramilitary organisations were forming, arms were being distributed to the people. In some parts of Yugoslavia civil authority was breaking down and people were frightened. So the build-up was occurring when I arrived. It was evident to everybody that there was potential here for a dreadful tragedy, but it was very difficult to -- to get the European Union particularly, and the United States, involved in trying to resolve this problem, to step in and ensure that the violence did not continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived and during your stay there, what was your assessment of the status of the Serbs in Croatia? I'm referring to the time period of your arrival in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, it was very worrisome. I mean, with the election of Mr. Tudjman and his party, when they won the election and declared essentially that they wanted to break away from Yugoslavia. He even had said that he would like to restore the old, historical Croatian boundaries, which included good parts of Bosnia. This -- his return of the old Ustasha symbols, the chequered flag, his actions in dismissing many of the Serbs from public jobs, public service, this frightened the Serbs in the -- that were living in Croatia, the 12 per cent of Serbs. There was, I think, very few of them who had not had their fathers or grandfathers subject to Ustashi genocide 50 years before, and it worried them to think that the events of April and early summer of 1941 could be repeated in -- in 1991. So they were frightened and very deeply concerned. And as we know, many of them took up arms and decided that if Croatia separated, that they did not want to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Yugoslavia and during your stay there, you spent most of your time in Belgrade, I assume, because that's where your embassy was and where you resided. Did you observe in Belgrade and in Serbia any kind of ethnic discrimination against anybody?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: No, I can't say I did. Belgrade was a modern, cosmopolitan city, with large ethnic groups of Albanians, of Muslims, of Romans, Gypsies. I certainly didn't notice any -- any discrimination or prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll take a look a few things now having to do with the -- what is called here the Kosovo indictment. In paragraph 75, it says that: "During the 1980s, Serbs voiced concern about discrimination against them by the Kosovo Albanian-led provincial government, while Kosovo Albanians voiced concern about economic underdevelopment and called for greater political liberalisation and republican status for Kosovo. From 1981 onwards, Kosovo Albanians staged demonstrations which were suppressed by SFRY military and police forces of Serbia." Now, to the best of your knowledge -- that's the end of that quotation. According to your knowledge and according to the information you had and what you knew about the situation - you spent two years there - are these allegations correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there are several -- several allegations. Let's take them one by one, Mr. Milosevic. The first one, it seems to me, is that the Serbs voiced concern about discrimination against them by the Kosovo Albanian-led provincial government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that. I didn't witness it personally, but I was aware that there had been complaints generally throughout the 1980s that the Serbs were, in effect, being pushed out of Kosovo by the actions of Albanians and that they felt threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the second one is that the Kosovo Albanians voiced concern about economic underdevelopment and called for greater political liberalisation and republican status for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was certainly aware of that. I mean, Kosovo was one of the poorest republics in the federation. I don't know what the per capita income was, but it was very low compared, for example, with Croatia and Slovenia. And on the other hand, I recall vividly going to visit Slovenia and meeting with the leader there who told me that they wished eventually to separate, and one of the primary reasons were they were fed up with having to spend all of their money subsidising Kosovo. I think that there's no question that the economic development of Kosovo was -- was, as I said, underdeveloped, but on the other hand, I would also suggest that the standard of living that was existing in Kosovo in the 1980s was probably better than is existing now, but that's a personal comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ambassador, you didn't comment on the republic status of Kosovo, and I'm afraid you said it was one of the republics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The republican status, it was always a desire on the part of the Albanians in Kosovo. They had been given, as we know, autonomous status, and in effect that was almost the same as being a republic but it wasn't quite a republican status, and they had always desired to be a republic of Yugoslavia. Their leader at the time, unofficial leader, Rugova, who unfortunately has passed away last month, as you know, was interested, I think, in not so much in becoming a republic but in becoming an independent country, and that was his -- his goal and his aim. But it was his goal and aim to do it by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the last allegation is that after 1981, Kosovo Albanians staged demonstrations, and these demonstrations were suppressed by the SFRY military and police forces of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I wasn't there at the time, but certainly whenever there was violence occurring, either in Kosovo or anywhere else in Yugoslavia, the security police would do their best to repress that and to stop it. And that was often done, as many observers have pointed out, with some degree of brutality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your comment there is recorded as whenever there was violence occurring.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the question was staged demonstrations, and these demonstrations were suppressed by the police forces and military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True, but often these demonstrations took a violent turn. I was in one myself in the middle of Belgrade in 1991, and the demonstrations in -- in the Balkans were not always peaceful, with people walking with placards. They also involved throwing stones and pavement and burning and pillaging and rioting. When that occurred, the police stepped in with considerable force. I've also seen demonstrations in Belgrade that were peaceful, by students who were walking with placards and demonstrating peacefully, and the police were not intervening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, you as the future ambassador to Yugoslavia in part of your mandate, term of office, you were appointed ambassador to the neighbouring country of Albania; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was also the ambassador -- Canadian ambassador to Albania, credited to Albania but situated in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you had an opportunity of becoming acquainted with Albania and to travel around Albania; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever make any comparison with respect to the situation in Albania and the situation in Kosovo? I'm not talking about Yugoslavia now, just the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. So when we're talking about Albanians primarily.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, one could not help but make comparisons. Albania at that time was extremely poor, I would think almost 90 per cent unemployment. On my first visit to Tirana, no one was working in the fields. The state farms had been abandoned, the machinery was rusting. In Tirana thousands of young men had nothing to do but walk about and hope they could get out of the country and to Italy. In comparison, Kosovo, of course the Albanians in Kosovo were very much better off and very often you would see Albanians from Kosovo in Albania driving their cars, quite well dressed, and spending their money. They were the envy, of course, of Albanians. Their standard of living, the ones in Kosovo, by Slovenian standards, were very low, but the Albanian standard compared to the Kosovo Albanians was equally bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 79 of the Kosovo indictment, among other things, it says the following: "In early 1989, the Serbian Assembly proposed amendments to the constitution of Serbia which would strip Kosovo most of its autonomous powers including ..." et cetera, et cetera, control of the police, education, and economic policy and choice of official language, as well as its veto powers over further changes to the constitution of Serbia. To the best of your knowledge, is that correct? On the basis of what you knew about what your colleagues in the diplomatic corps knew about, are these allegations correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, the allegation is correct that Kosovo lost its veto power over legislation in Serbia, but my own experience at the time in 1990 was that the Albanians had chosen as a result -- as a protest to losing their autonomy or their veto power, to withdraw from the federal institutions. They refused to pay their income tax, they were running their own educational and health services to a degree. They were still getting their social services and pensions, the ones that had -- deserved them from the federal government, but basically there was an impasse. They simply did not wish to participate any more in the elections that were held or to attend the parliamentary sessions. They simply withdrew and set up their own parallel organisations. The fact of the matter is that the Yugoslav federation authorities also in effect withdrew. They did not bother with them very much. There was very little interference, while I was there, from federal institutions, other than keeping law and order in the province. But there was certainly very little violence occurring, if any, and it wasn't really until 1998, long after I had left, that the KLA emerged when the violence in Kosovo began to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just stay on this issue for a moment. In paragraph 87, it says: "At the end of the 1990s -- throughout late 1990 and 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanian doctors, teachers, professors, workers, police and civil servants were dismissed from their positions." Now, you were there at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they were not dismissed. They simply voluntarily withdrew from their positions. Continued to do the work but under a sort of underground parallel government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was your knowledge -- what was your knowledge based on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reports that I would get from our officers who would go to Kosovo to talk to people, my own discussions with some Albanian delegations who would come to Belgrade, conversations with fellow diplomats. And that's essentially how I would find out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And of course you would have been sending to your headquarters reports on the situation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- In Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the reports that you would have sent would have borne this out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember how many were sent but they would try to describe the situation as it was -- occurred, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, in paragraph 91, it says that: "Slobodan Milosevic had control over the federal government as well as the republican government and the individuals with whom the international community negotiated ..." and so on and so forth. Now, at the time that you yourself were in Belgrade, who was the Prime Minister of the federal government? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic. In putting that paragraph, you omitted the word "de facto." I think if you're going to put it, you should put it fully. The allegation is that you had de facto control over the federal government as well as the republican government.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was president of the Republic of Serbia at that time, as you know, Mr. Bissett, and it says here that I exercised de facto control over the federal government. Now, you were there yourself in Belgrade at that critical time. Is that true? Did I have de facto control of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I mean what does "de facto control" mean? As far as I'm concerned, I saw no evidence of that. I think the -- if you take the example of the federal army, I think the federal army was -- was under the control of the federal authorities. As far as I was concerned as an ambassador - and I think most other ambassadors believe this - we followed the rules and we dealt with the federal authorities when we were dealing with federal issues concerning the army, and we dealt with the presidents of the various republics when we were dealing with issues that concerned them. That began, I must say, later on when the fighting broke open and there was disintegration of many of the federal functions. That was a changing situation. And it was sometimes difficult to know who was in control, if anybody was, of some of the functions that were being carried out by government in Yugoslavia. But at the time that I was there, certainly there was a clear distinction between the federal authorities and the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, the other side over there, in keeping with their rules, provided me with some of your telegrams, and they are marked in the materials. There's an attached letter, cable from Canadian Ambassador James Bissett, Canadian government, regarding meeting with Milosevic. Unfortunately before I ask you this question, Mr. Bissett, I received only three telegrams in actual fact. Just tell me for comparison purposes, roughly speaking -- I know you can't give an exact number, but roughly speaking, how many telegrams did you send during your term of office in Yugoslavia from the end of 1990 until mid-1992 when you left the country?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I sent a lot of telegrams. Certainly more than three. I can't even make an estimate. It was the custom in our embassy, of course, for the political officers to send telegrams. They sent the bulk of the telegrams. I did not sign them. It was usually customary, if there was a very important event or issue or where I had gone to visit an important official or make a demarche, as they say in diplomatic language, that I would write my own telegrams and sign them, but how many, I would think three or four, maybe, a week or something along that nature. It also depended a good deal, of course, on staff at the embassy, holidays and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But that would be three or four a week, would it, roughly, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes. And that would vary from week to week, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now throughout your period here, your term of office, we only have this very limited number, but I will try, from what you wrote there in the telegram -- and you can find the telegram in tab 1 among your documents, the ones you have before you. Have you found it, Mr. Bissett?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in your telegram, you say what I did for a short time before the meeting. You said: "... in the early hours of the morning [In English] affixed his signature to the EEC declaration permitting EEC observers to operate in Croatia and agreeing to an international conference on Yugoslav political crisis." [Interpretation] What declaration was this? What agreement that you mention here in your telegram with respect to me?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: This was a declaration calling for the disarmament of the Serbian forces that were fighting in Croatia against the Croatian forces. Calling for disarmament and withdrawal of Croatian forces from the parts of Croatia occupied by the Serbs, a withdrawal of the fighting forces, and the storing of arms, as I recall, under a shared key arrangement, and a cease-fire, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of the European observers coming in - because at the time it was still the European Community - on the territory, or what territory did they come into and what was their task? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as I recall, the European observers, it was part of the declaration to have European observers in the Serbian populated areas of Croatia, to offer them protection and to ensure that they were not engaging in conflict with their Croatian opponents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you say that you express satisfaction, and I quote what you've said here, what you wrote in your telegram: "[In English] That Serbia had, along with other republics and Yugoslavia federal government, agreed to terms of EEC declaration."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Bissett, you mention here the other republics. You mention the federal government. Now, I should like to remind you of the paragraph that I read out to you a moment ago and a portion of that paragraph, saying that I exercised de facto control of the federal government as well as the republican government and was the person with whom the international community negotiated a variety of peace plans and agreements related, et cetera. So you say that the EC declaration, that Serbia took part and the federal government took part. Does this agree with what I read out and what you wrote in your telegram? Is that the same thing?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was it, then, that took part in the adoption of the declaration? Was it just Serbia, or did all the republics take part on an equal footing, including the federal government? Did Serbia have any separate or special position in that regard or did it take part on a footing of equality with the other republics, and does the federal government appear there as the federal power and authority?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, in the case of the federal government, of course they were there in that capacity as still Yugoslavia existed at the time, and as -- to my knowledge, all of the other republics participated, but I cannot swear to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to speak in your telegram of our talk, and I'm going to quote the next portion. You say that I pointed out the misunderstanding by EEC "[In English] of differences dividing Serbs and Croatians and apparent decision by EEC misunderstanding."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what reasons did I give you for what I said about this misunderstanding? You say here "... misunderstanding by the EEC about differences dividing Serbia and Croat and apparent decision by EEC misunderstanding."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I think it's explained further in the telegram that your concern was that the EEC representatives had oversimplified the situation that was taking place and the conflict that was going on in Croatia between the Serb and the Croatian population there, and that they had from the beginning taken a position that Serbia was to blame for this. And that, I think, was your concern, that already the EEC, who had stepped in to mediate in an objective fashion, were already showing that they were biased against Serbia and the federal government. And you also expressed concern, particularly about the Germans, that their foreign minister at the time, Genscher, would not listen to any of the points of view or positions presented by the Serbian side. So you were telling me at the time, as I recall, that you had signed the document in the interests of helping negotiate a peaceful settlement there and an end to the fighting but you were not entirely happy that the European Community seemed to be blaming Serbia for everything that was going wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me this: In view of your experience and the knowledge you had of those times, according to that knowledge and information, did oversimplification of media presentation of events actually exist, et cetera? Is that something that actually existed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: I think it definitely did exist, and I think it was part of the problem that was going to ensue throughout the negotiations in Yugoslavia. Right from the beginning, from the time the federal army was sent by the federal Prime Minister into Slovenia, the major news media around the world interpreted that as the big bullying Serb-led army is attacking poor Slovenia. And I think from the outset the media presentation of events in Yugoslavia presented the Serbs as the villains and the others as the good guys, and it was an oversimplification designed, of course, for the modern media, television, which can present a minute and a half at the most of presentation of extremely complicated events, and there's a tendency to do it in very stark terms of good guy, bad guy. I think that was an oversimplification from the beginning and it haunted Yugoslavia from that day on in terms of trying to get objective mediation between the quarreling parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, do you say that there was a general direction or an original point from which this media oversimplification to the detriment of the Serbs came?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I mean, it's my personal view, but I remember watching the television presented by CNN at the outbreak of hostilities in Slovenia, and I think very clearly, even though James Baker, the Secretary of State at the time, had told the federal Prime Minister - who was a Croatian, by the way - Markovic, that if the Slovenes did break away, there was -- and he sent the army in to try and resolve the issue, that the United States would not -- would not condemn them. This is hearsay evidence, I'm afraid, but I've heard it from the US ambassador at the time, Mr. Zimmerman. But despite that, the television presentation in the United States clearly from that -- from the first two or three days, presented it as basically as a Serb-led federal army invading poor little Slovenia, and that was -- that was the public perception from there on in, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the understanding of these events that you mention in your telegram which were the subject of discussion between you and me at the time and which related to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I think what you mean there is that you had pointed out that the oversimplification was taking place and without a full knowledge of the history of the Balkans and the history of what had happened in Yugoslavia during the Second World War. And we discussed that, that part of the problem was that a lot of the negotiators who had come in to mediate peace were not aware that genocide had in fact taken place in Croatian during World War II when -- the figures are disputed, but minimally 700.000 Serbs, Jews, and Gypsies had been subject to death. And it was, therefore, of great concern to you that the international mediator should be aware of the sensitivities these historical events had and the impact they had on the psychology of the Serbs who were living in Croatia, and you felt that there was not that clear understanding and that it wasn't a question of Serbs wanting to join Serbia, it was a question of Serbs being very frightened by the idea that Mr. Tudjman's regime might repeat what had happened in 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, is it your view, based on your experiences at the time, that the way all these events were reported in the media was distorted?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Yes. It is clearly my view that they were distorted. Not only in the media but the European Community that was coming in to mediate this dispute had also threatened sanctions against Serbia and the federal government. There was no mention of sanctions against Croatia; the sanctions were going to be applied to Serbia. And I think from the outset there was this -- this bias and this distortion, and it made the situation in attempting to achieve peace much more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, last question before we break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bissett, according to your knowledge, what was the cause and origin of this kind of partial and distorted media reporting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BISSETT
utterances.text: Well, I mean that's a very difficult question. I think I tried to explain it. In the media reporting, it's simply that today's journalists do not have time to go into the history of the Balkans. Most North American media hadn't the slightest idea where Kosovo was and had never heard of some of these places that were suddenly in the news. They had a very short period of time to report events, and they did it very quickly, and so it was an oversimplification. I don't think that -- necessarily blaming them but they don't have time to do historical research before they put the TV programme on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bissett. Mr. Milosevic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just want to say that I was not aware until I arrived in The Hague that these telegrams were here, but -- I mean, I might not have chosen these ones, there may have been others I would have chosen, but they were supplied, I imagine, by my former bosses in the Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may have a chance later to refer to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, don't misunderstanding me, I now have a copy of them, I've read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, the others that are not here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you wish to tender tabs 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They are admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the collection of documents for the witness will be Exhibit D335.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are adjourned until tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Mr. Milosevic, I am to inform you that the appointment with the doctor has now been fixed for 5.00 p.m. today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
